name: Text to Video, Physics and Continuity
title: Text to Video, Physics and Continuity
answer: Text to video covers systems that turn a written prompt into a moving image sequence, and the two hard problems that decide whether the result is usable: physics and continuity. Physics means objects fall, collide, spill and deform in ways a viewer accepts without thinking, and continuity means a character, a prop or a light source stays consistent from one shot to the next. In cinematography the interest is practical, because a generated clip only earns its place if it can sit beside live footage or carry a scene on its own. The field sits between film craft and generative modelling, and the people working in it are usually directors, editors, VFX artists and technical artists rather than researchers.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on diffusion models trained on large collections of video, usually paired with a text encoder that turns the prompt into conditioning the model can follow. Training and inference both lean on GPU clusters, and long clips are normally produced in short segments that are then joined, extended or interpolated. Practitioners rarely touch the training stack; they work through hosted services or local interfaces such as ComfyUI, and they steer results with prompts, reference images, control signals and seed values. Storage and review matter more than they sound, because a single shot can generate dozens of candidate takes before one is kept.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pass starts with a written shot description, often broken into subject, action, camera move and lighting, then a first generation at low resolution to test the motion. Artists then refine with image or video references, control inputs for pose and depth, and repeated short extensions that carry the action forward. Continuity is checked by eye against the previous shot, and physics is judged by whether weight, contact and momentum read correctly, since a floating foot or a melting hand breaks the illusion faster than a soft texture. Fixes range from re-rolling the seed to repainting a few frames, compositing a real element, or cutting around the failure in the edit.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions cluster around the training data, the prompt, and the output, and practice varies by studio and jurisdiction. Many productions keep a record of prompts, seeds, model versions and reference assets so a shot can be reproduced or defended later, and some require that generated material be labelled or kept separate from camera original. Likeness and voice are sensitive areas, and consent from performers or estates is often handled contractually rather than technically. Provenance tooling such as C2PA and watermarking is increasingly requested by distributors, though adoption is uneven. None of this is legal advice, and terms differ between the services used.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The near term is less about longer clips and more about control: consistent characters across shots, reliable camera moves, and physical behaviour that survives a cut. Expect tighter coupling between generation and the edit, with tools that hold a scene's look and blocking rather than producing isolated fragments. Evaluation is likely to stay human, since continuity and physical plausibility are judged by watching, not by a score. As the outputs improve, the craft question shifts from whether a shot can be generated to whether it belongs in the film.
